chapter: The Latin scene and business of the 1940s-70s
title: Invisible Latin musicians
summary: He says Latin musicians are overlooked and he protects Machito's band.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Yeah. I've noticed -- I mean, it seems to be a permanent problem in that you've got anywhere between one and seven and one and ten New Yorkers, depending on who you believe is Spanish-speaking, about one in 7.5. And yet, I mean, I've noticed the Latin musicians are what you might call the invisible men of American music. Take yourself, -- I mean, the musicians know you but when I talk to jazz people, they don't know anything about it.
Look at (unintelligible), for that matter. Who knows? (Unintelligible) played for three years in the Cotton Club with his band.
You won't find his name anywhere in the index, you won't find your name anywhere in the index of the jazz book.
But Chito, because of the connection with --
And it seems to be that it's still going on. If it's Latin, you don't hear about it.

That's it. (Unintelligible). Even with this now, with this house that we're in now, what (unintelligible) to me? When I left __________, all these hypocrite people in New York (unintelligible). And I said, no, no, don't talk that way because I don't want nobody to talk that way about Chito, because that's my band. I created that band and as long as I live and that band live, it's me. So I don't want to hear that. I (unintelligible) another band to compete with Chito. That's my band.
(Unintelligible) and I'm going to find my way of living (unintelligible). What happened with that?
